paragraphs.source_en: When I looked, he seemed to be a student of about eighteen or nineteen, around Miss Yukie’s age. His large head was cropped so close that the scalp almost showed through, and a bulbous nose sat squarely in the middle of his face. He sat quietly in a corner of the parlor; though he had no feature especially worth mentioning, his skull looked remarkably large. If his head looked so big even with his hair cut that short, it would surely draw still more attention if he wore a long parted hairstyle like my master’s. According to my master’s usual theory, anyone with such a big head is certain to be no good at his studies. That may be true, yet at first glance he looked quite grand, almost like Napoleon. He wore the ordinary dress of a student: whether it was Satsuma, Kurume, or Iyo kasuri I could not tell, but at any rate it was a short-sleeved lined robe of some striped cloth, and underneath he seemed to have on neither shirt nor under-robe. They say a bare lined robe and bare feet make for a stylishly dashing appearance, but this young man gave off a decidedly slovenly impression. In particular, the three clear big-toe marks on the tatami, exactly like those left when the thief came in last time, were entirely the fault of those bare feet. He had planted himself properly on top of the fourth barefoot print, sitting in a painfully constrained posture. Of course there is nothing odd in a person who ought to show respect sitting meekly and properly; but for this cropped-headed ruffian in a too-short jacket to sit there in such affected humility was altogether incongruous. He was the sort who took pride in not bowing even when he met a teacher on the road; to make him sit like an ordinary person for thirty minutes would surely be torture. Yet now he posed as though born a modest gentleman or a venerable man of virtue, and however painful it was for him, to an onlooker it was exceedingly funny. When one thinks that someone who usually makes such a racket in the classroom or on the playground possesses such power to restrain himself, he seems both pitiable and comic. Sitting face to face like this, even my normally dull-witted master seemed to exert some pressure upon a student. My master was probably rather proud of it too. As the saying goes, dust piled up becomes a mountain; insignificant students, once gathered in a crowd, may become a body not to be trifled with, perhaps even launching an exclusion movement or a strike. But this is much like the way a coward grows bold after drinking. Thus it is fair to say that relying on strength in numbers and breaking into disorder is the result of a man’s spirit becoming intoxicated by the crowd and losing its sober sense. Otherwise this youth in striped cloth, now not so much terrified as silently shrinking back before the sliding screen, could hardly despise or make a fool of a teacher, however decrepit that teacher might be, so long as he bore the name.

paragraphs.source_zh: 我一看，大概是个十八九岁、年龄和雪江姑娘相仿的学生。他的大脑袋头发剪得特别短，短得头皮都似乎露了出来，蒜头鼻子占据在面孔当中。他在客厅的角落里肃静地坐着，虽然他缺少值得一提的特征，但他的头盖骨却显得非常大。他的头发剪得那么短，头还显得如此之大，如果像主人那样也留个长长的分头，那就更加惹人注目啦。按主人的一贯说法，具有这样一个大脑袋的人，学业肯定是不会好的。这也许是事实，不过乍看起来活像个仪表堂堂的拿破仑，他穿的是一般学生经常穿的服装，虽然分不清是萨摩条纹布，还是久留米条纹布或是伊予条纹布，总之是件用条纹布做成的、袖子很短的夹袍，里边好像既没有穿衬衫也没有穿套衣。尽管人们都说光身穿夹袍和光着脚是一种风流潇洒的打扮，不过这个年轻人却给人一种松松垮垮的感觉。尤其是铺席上印有三处和上次小偷进来时一模一样的大拇脚趾印迹，这完全应归咎于他那双赤脚。他规规矩矩地坐在了第四处赤脚印的上边，采取的是很拘谨的坐姿。说起来，那种应该向对方表示敬意的人，采取端坐姿势并不显得别扭，但是像这样一个身穿短腚袄，剃着和尚头的闹将，居然也装模作样地坐在那里，就显得非常不协调了。他本来是个在路上遇着老师都以不敬礼为荣的那种人，如果让他和正常人一样坐上三十分钟对他肯定也是活受罪。但他现在却装得好像谦谦君子或盛德长者一般，尽管受罪得很，但在旁人看来仍然十分滑稽可笑。一想到他是那种平常在教室里或操场上闹翻天的人，居然会有如此约束自己的能力，就觉得他既可怜又可笑。这样面对面地相视而坐，即使平时是愚呆的主人，这时也会对学生多少产生点压力。主人大概也很为此得意吧。常言说：“积尘则成山”，微不足道的一些学生一旦成群结伙，就会成为不可侮的团体，也许会搞出排斥运动或罢课来的。但是这种现象正像胆小鬼喝了酒以后就会胆子大起来一样的。因此，可以认为那种仗恃人多势众，胡乱闹腾，正是人的精神陷入迷乱的结果，从而失掉了清醒头脑的缘故。否则的话，像现在这位与其说是惶恐不安倒不如说是悄然无声地退缩在隔扇前边的穿条纹布的青年人，不管老师是怎样的老朽，既然名为老师，他就不能看不起老师，也不能耍弄老师。

paragraphs.source_en: My master pushed a cushion toward the visitor and said, “Please spread it out,” but the cropped-headed fellow stiffly answered, “Yes,” and still did not move. The cotton cushion lay right before him; naturally it did not say, “Please sit on me,” while behind it the cropped fellow’s great head sat motionless, which was truly amusing. A cushion, after all, was bought by my master’s wife at the industrial fair for people to sit on, not for people to stare at. If no one sits on a cushion, the cushion’s honor is plainly damaged, and of course the face of the master who urged his guest to sit on it must also suffer somewhat. This cropped-headed gentleman, who would rather ruin my master’s face than cease glaring at the cushion, certainly did not dislike the cushion itself. To tell the truth, he had almost never in his life sat formally on a cushion, except at his grandfather’s memorial service. So his legs, numb from kneeling, had already begun to complain. Even so, he would not sit on it. Though the cushion waited there idle, he would not sit on it; though my master had plainly said, “Please spread it out,” he still refused. What a troublesome cropped-headed fellow! If he was going to be this polite, he might have shown a little more politeness when they gathered in groups, a little more in class, and a little more when living at his boarding house. He is considerate where there is no need to be, but when he ought to be modest he is not; instead he raises havoc. A bad-natured cropped-headed rogue indeed!
